{"requestId":"4220b0f6164cbfbc33df58cf383ce9f0","resolvedSearchType":"","results":[{"id":"https://www.electronicsbrief.com/articles/is-the-ai-boom-over-follow-the-debt-then-the-machines","title":"Is the AI boom over? Follow the debt, then the machines","url":"https://www.electronicsbrief.com/articles/is-the-ai-boom-over-follow-the-debt-then-the-machines","publishedDate":"2026-10-15T00:00:00.000Z","author":"James Creber","text":"Is the AI boom over? Follow the debt, then the machines\n\n# Is the AI boom over? Follow the debt, then the machines\n\nCoreWeave, IREN and other infrastructure stocks have taken a beating. Their financial results and ASML’s order outlook show why the answer is more complicated than a falling share-price chart.\n\nBy\n\nJames Creber\n\n15 October 2026\n\nIllustrative image: Taylor Vick on Unsplash\n\nThe AI building boom has acquired an awkward companion: a much closer examination of the bill.\n\nWednesday’s selling caught companies across the infrastructure chain. In Reuters’ intraday report on 14 October, Nebius was down 15.1%, CoreWeave 9.5%, IREN 9.9% and Applied Digital 8.8%. These were snapshots during trading, rather than closing prices.\n\n“Investors are questioning whether the AI buildout will generate the returns that were expected,” Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners, told Reuters. [Source 1]\n\nThat question has teeth. Building a computing business means paying for machines, power and buildings before all the corresponding revenue arrives. If financing becomes more expensive, the customers can remain enthusiastic while the economics for the infrastructure owner become less comfortable.\n\nThe distinction is visible in the companies’ own accounts.\n\n## CoreWeave’s interest bill is already substantial\n\nCoreWeave reported second-quarter revenue of $2.575bn, against $1.212bn a year earlier. Chief executive Michael Intrator said: “Customer demand is accelerating.”\n\nThe same quarter contained $640m of net interest expense and a $626m net loss. Net interest expense was equivalent to approximately a quarter of revenue.\n\nIts adjusted EBITDA of $1.510bn gives a different view of operating performance, but that measure excludes interest and other substantial costs. It cannot settle the question of what remains for shareholders after the infrastructure has been financed.\n\nCoreWeave also reported approximately $104bn of revenue backlog at the end of June. The company’s definition makes delivery and service availability conditions explicit. That is valuable contracted business, but the backlog has to be converted into an operating service before the associated revenue can be recognised. [Source 2]\n\nThe scheduling problem underneath those figures is familiar to anyone who has commissioned complex equipment. Spending begins before acceptance. Delays can stretch the interval between paying for an asset and earning from it.\n\nFinancial leverage makes that interval more consequential. As a simple illustration, an additional three percentage points of annual interest on $1bn of borrowing represents $30m a year. That is arithmetic, not a forecast for CoreWeave, but it explains why a change in the price of money can alter the value of a project without changing the number of customers asking for compute.\n\n## IREN shows why the contract matters\n\nIREN’s transition also needs to be read through actual revenue and financing terms.\n\nFor the financial year ended June 2026, it reported $128.8m of AI cloud revenue and $578.2m from bitcoin mining. The historical revenue mix therefore still reflected the business it was moving away from.\n\nIts financing disclosures show different economics within the new business. IREN reported $3.6bn of investment-grade GPU financing associated with its Microsoft contract at a weighted average interest rate of 6%, excluding fees.\n\nA separate $2.4bn financing led by Blue Owl and PIMCO for its Mackenzie air-cooled expansion carried a fixed rate of 9%. That deployment served non-investment-grade customers.\n\nThe facilities have different structures and counterparties, so the rates are not interchangeable measures of IREN’s overall borrowing cost. They do demonstrate that the customer behind the GPU deployment matters to its financing. [Source 3]\n\nThere is a second distinction inside the growth figures. Contracted annualised run-rate revenue describes a level of business under specified operating assumptions. It is not the revenue already earned during a financial year. Commissioning, testing and customer acceptance sit between the contract and the realised result.\n\nA market can become less willing to pay today for that future conversion without concluding that the contracted workload has disappeared.\n\n## The equipment supplier is telling another part of the story\n\nASML’s latest results make a blanket declaration that the AI boom is over difficult to sustain.\n\nThe lithography equipment maker reported third-quarter sales of €11.7bn and net income of €5bn. More significantly for the capacity argument, it said its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 would not fully meet customer demand.\n\nChief executive Christophe Fouquet said that “some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030”.\n\nASML is investigating additional 2028 capacity beyond the increase it had previously communicated. Customer interest extending into later years is not the same as completed orde","highlights":["The AI building boom has acquired an awkward companion: a much closer examination of the bill.\n\nWednesday’s selling caught companies across the infrastructure chain. The historical revenue mix therefore still reflected the business it was moving away from.\n\nIts financing disclosures show different economics within the new business. That deployment served non-investment-grade customers.\n\nThe facilities have different structures and counterparties, so the rates are not interchangeable measures of IREN’s overall borrowing cost. Investors question whether AI infrastructure projects will deliver expected returns as debt becomes pricier.\n- IREN (IREN Limited) is highlighted as a case study: in the year ending June 2026 it posted AI cloud revenue of $128.8M but $578.2M from bitcoin mining, signaling a shift in business mix.\n- IREN’s financing shows varied costs depending on counterparty and project:\n  - $3.6B in non-investment-grade customers.\n- These differing financing terms illustrate how the profitability of AI infrastructure depends on who the customer is and the debt structure behind GPU turmoil: neoclouds struggle, credit risks jump, Solidigm pulls IPO\n\n# Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO\n\nPublished Fri, Oct 23 2026 5:49 PM EDT Updated Sat, Oct 24 2026 2:41 AM EDT\n\nIsabel O'Brien@in/xisabelobrienx@xisabelobrienx\n\nKey Points\n\n- Concerns over the AI trade dragged the Nasdaq down this week, with neoclouds posting some of the steepest losses.\n- Debt markets are roiling, with Meta, Oracle and Nvidia facing the largest-ever spreads on credit default swaps linked to their corporate bonds. \n- SK Hynix abandoned plans for an IPO of its Solidigm unit. \n\nCoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 28, 2025.\n\nMichael M. Santiago | Getty Images\n\nNeoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta Add To Watchlist turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Add To Watchlist Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.\n\nIt's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade. \n\nThe Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet Add To Watchlist, shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.\n\nWhile the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence buildout is showing signs of strain. \n\nShares of neoclouds CoreWeave Add To Watchlist, Nebius Add To Watchlist and IREN Add To Watchlist all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default. \n\nMeanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%. \n\n\"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud\" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's \"Squawk on the Street\" on Thursday.\n\nVIDEO 2:58 02:58\n\nFears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast. \n\nAI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.\n\nAnalysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.\n\nNvidia Add To Watchlist CEO Jensen Huang, perhaps the leading AI evangelist, remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that \"demand for the neoclouds is off the charts.\"\n\n\"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital,\" Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal. \"That's going to get solved.\"\n\n## Withdrawn IPO\n\nWall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix Add To Watchlist, one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel Add To Watchlist in 2021.\n\n\"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends,\" SK Hynix said in a release. \n\nDespite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.\n\nMeta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.\n\nMeta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements. \n\nSpreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia Add To Watchlist and Oracle Add To Watchlist also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. The yield on a CoreWeave bond maturing in 2032 hit nearly 15% on Tuesday, up about 1.5 percentage points over the past week, the Financial Times reported. Other AI cloud providers fell with it. Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) dropped 10.05% and IREN (NASDAQ:IREN) lost 9.57%. \n\nThe concern is the debt load. CoreWeave has raised more than $35 billion this year through chip-backed loans, high-yield bonds, convertibles and share sales, taking its debt and lease obligations to about $52 billion at the end of June. Interest costs more than doubled from a year earlier to $640 million in the second quarter, and debt stood at about 5.8x annualized second-quarter EBITDA. S&P rates its financial risk as aggressive. \n\nCreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin told the FT the bonds have sold off on worries about a mismatch between CoreWeave's long data center leases and its shorter customer contracts. If there's an overbuild, why would [customers] renew their contract with CoreWeave? he said. Analysts expect negative free cash flow of about $25 billion this year, according to Visible Alpha. (Photo by Cheng Xin/Getty Images)\n\nAnushka Basu· Stocktwits\n\nPublished Oct 20, 2026 | 7:43 AM EDT\n\n- After recent pressure on the IREN stock, co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers are supported fully by cash, and the company had no debt against assets.\n- Under recent three-year contracts, customer prepayments cover 45% to 55% of GPU expenses, Roberts said.\n- IREN's Microsoft agreement covered 96% of GPU expenses, with prepayments at 6%, and non-investment payment-grade customers paid 9%.\n\nShares of IREN Limited (IREN) edged lower in pre-market trading on Tuesday after co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers did not carry any debt. Roberts responded to investors' concern over how the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud providers will fund their expansion.\n\nRoberts said on X that IREN has paid for their data center construction in cash so far. Adding to it, he said that the sites can support their own financing once they come online with contracted customers. Robert laid out the process step by step. Customers must first sign multi-year take-or-pay contracts, which require payment whether or not they use the capacity. On recent three-year deals, he said prepayments covered 45% to 55% of the cost of the graphics processing units (GPUs).\n\nDeepti Sri\n\nSource: @danroberts0101/x\n\nHe added that lenders mostly fund the rest, with the GPUs serving as collateral. Robert added that Iren's Microsoft (MSFT) contract was supported by an A-rated facility at 6% or so. That, plus prepayments, accounts for 96% of the GPU spending. One customer without an investment-grade rating at Iren's McKenzie site in British Columbia was borrowing at a fixed 9%. \n\nThe loan and prepayment more than pay for the whole cost of the GPU, the co-CEO added. He acknowledged that future debt will price at whatever the market charges. But he said a payback of about 2 years on recent contracts means \"a wider spread barely moves the economics.\"\n\n## Demand Outruns Build Capacity\n\nAccording to Roberts, customer demand exceeds what IREN can build. The company's 2026 capacity is largely sold out, he added, saying recent 3-year contracts are priced at more than double last year's level. Demand for capacity arriving in 2027 is several times oversubscribed, and discussions on 2028 have begun. The holdup in the industry is not signing deals, he said. Getting GPUs online is the issue, as announced capacity keeps sleeping across the sector.\n\n## Pressure On Neocoloud Stocks Continue\n\nNeoclouds, the specialized AI cloud providers, have been under pressure through the past week. The stock has been down over 20% over the past week. Investors became increasingly worried after debt pressures at CoreWeave (CRWV) and a research firm warned that over 80% of neoclouds might no longer be able to operate independently by 2030.\n\n## Retail Chatter For IREN Surges \n\nIREN stock was down over 4% in pre-market trade, trading at $26. On Stocktwits retail sentiment around IREN remained in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone, with ‘high’ chatter levels over the past day. According to platform data, chatter around IREN has been up over 952% over the past 30 days.\n\nOne user on Stocktwits said that the IREN stock had erased all of the previous day's gain, and it would need to rise 70% to reach above $46 again. \n\nFor updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com.","highlights":["# IREN Co-CEO Daniel Roberts Says Firm’s Data Centers Carry No Debt As Funding Worries Hit Stock\n\nIREN shares slipped over 4% in pre-market trade on Tuesday amid broader pressure on new cloud firms.\n\nIn this photo illustration, a person holds a smartphone displaying the logo of Iren Energy Limited. (Photo by Cheng Xin/Getty Images)\n\nAnushka Basu· Stocktwits\n\nPublished Oct 20, 2026 | 7:43 AM EDT\n\n- After recent pressure on the IREN stock, co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers are supported fully by cash, and the company had no debt against assets.\n- Under recent three-year contracts, customer prepayments cover 45% to 55% of GPU expenses, Roberts said.\n- IREN's Microsoft agreement covered 96% of GPU expenses, with prepayments at 6%, and non-investment payment-grade customers paid 9%.\n\nShares of IREN Limited (IREN) edged lower in pre-market trading on Tuesday after co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers did not carry any debt. Adding to it, he said that the sites can support their own financing once they come online with contracted customers. Robert laid out the process step by step. Customers must first sign multi-year take-or-pay contracts, which require payment whether or not they use the capacity. On recent three-year deals, he said prepayments covered 45% to 55% of the cost of the graphics processing units (GPUs).\n\nDeepti Sri\n\nSource: @danroberts0101/x\n\nHe added that lenders mostly fund the rest, with the GPUs serving as collateral. Getting GPUs online is the issue, as announced capacity keeps sleeping across the sector.\n\n...\n\n## Pressure On Neocoloud Stocks Continue\n\nNeoclouds, the specialized AI cloud providers, have been under pressure through the past week. The stock has been down over 20% over the past week. Capex is largely prepaid via multi-year take-or-pay contracts, with 45–55% of GPU costs covered by prepayments on three-year deals. Remaining funding comes from lenders, using GPUs as collateral.\n- Microsoft deal and credit: IREN’s Microsoft-backed GPU spending is 96% funded by a mix of prepayments (6%) and a lender facility; one non-investment-grade customer at the McKenzie site borrows at ~9%.\n- Economics and payback: The combined loan and prepayment cover the full GPU cost; projected payback on recent contracts around ~2 years. Future debt rates will reflect market conditions, but current contracts keep economics favorable despite broader debt concerns.\n- Demand vs. capacity: Demand far outstrips IREN’s capacity. 2026 capacity is largely sold out; three-year contracts priced well above last year; 2027 capacity oversubscribed and discussions for 2028 have begun. The bottleneck is bringing GPUs online, not deal signings.\n- Market context: Neocloud/AI cloud stocks remain under pressure amid industry debt concerns (e.g., CoreWeave) and caution about independent operation viability for many neoclouds by 2030. IREN-specific exposure appears limited to its funded, contracted capacity and cash-based buildout.\n\nBottom line: IREN argues robust, cash-supported data-center financing with high prepayments and lender-backed GPU funding, mitigating near-term debt concerns even as broader neocloud funding worries and strong demand push pushouts in GPU deployments.","image":"https://news.stocktwits-cdn.com/large_Getty_Images_2232147678_jpg_9e7c3ea177.webp"},{"id":"https://www.ad-hoc-news.de/boerse/news/unternehmensnachrichten/iren-s-cash-funded-build-out-meets-a-market-that-wants-receipts/70377476","title":"IREN's Cash-Funded Build-Out Meets a Market That Wants Receipts","url":"https://www.ad-hoc-news.de/boerse/news/unternehmensnachrichten/iren-s-cash-funded-build-out-meets-a-market-that-wants-receipts/70377476","publishedDate":"2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z","author":"Rafael Müller","text":"IREN's Cash-Funded Build-Out Meets a Market That Wants Receipts\n\n# IREN's Cash-Funded Build-Out Meets a Market That Wants Receipts\n\n Published on 10/20/2026 at 20:40 | Editorial boerse-global.de \n\nIREN dropped 3.8% amid sector-wide AI infrastructure selling; co-CEO says data centre construction was cash-funded with no debt on those sites.\n\n \n\n \n\nIREN's Cash-Funded Build-Out Meets a Market That Wants Receipts Illustration mit AI erstellt.\n\nIREN shares fell 3.8% on the day as renewed selling hit AI data centre and so-called neocloud providers, with worries about oil-driven inflation and higher interest rates setting the tone. The move came alongside a broader retreat in AI-linked equities and a rebound in crude prices that weighed on US markets, according to Reuters. That is a sector backdrop, not a fresh company disclosure — an important line to draw, because shared selling pressure explains the direction of a stock without settling anything about its own risks.\n\n## Two Questions the Market Is Really Asking\n\nThe funding debate has been building since 14 October, when Reuters reported selling in AI infrastructure names amid rising rate expectations and named IREN among them. Investors were fretting over two things at once: how the build-out gets financed, and whether the AI spending will actually deliver the returns promised. Those questions are related but not the same. Strong demand does not answer the profitability question, and a financed site does not automatically answer the question about the terms of further growth. Reading every dip as doubt about the AI trend alone misses half the story.\n\nCo-CEO Daniel Roberts pushed back on the funding worries on Thursday, telling media that IREN paid for its data centre construction in cash and carries no debt against those sites. The statement matters, but so does its scope: it covers construction and the sites themselves, and it does not amount to blanket reassurance on every financing question. The market's concern is the capital-hungry expansion as a whole; Roberts' answer concerns specific IREN assets. Both can stand side by side without one fully refuting the other.\n\n## Gartner's Warning Lands on the Sector\n\nSentiment took a further knock from a Gartner forecast published on Thursday. The research firm reckons more than 80% of neocloud providers — the GPU rental specialists — could lose their independence by 2030. Media reports said the assessment intensified selling pressure on IREN and its peers. That does not translate into a specific fate for IREN, and losing independence is not the same as shutting down operations. Treating the forecast as proof against the individual company would be wrong. So would ignoring the scepticism about the sector model it reflects just because the stock had a good day.\n\n## Reliability Is the Other Test\n\nBeyond the balance sheet, technical reliability is under scrutiny. On 7 October, criticism surfaced about IREN's older Prince George and Mackenzie data centres in British Columbia. Customers reportedly flagged multi-day power outages, network disruptions, storage problems and difficulties with cooling and air quality. The report distinguished those sites from the newer Texas facilities — a caveat that counts, since criticism of individual data centres is not a verdict on every IREN site. Even a site with settled financing has to perform in operation. Those reported problems are not a sideshow to the rate debate; they bear on a different precondition for turning built infrastructure into a commercially convincing offering.\n\n## Redbank: A Blueprint, Not Capacity\n\nOn Thursday, IREN opened public consultation for its planned Redbank data centre campus near Wagga Wagga in New South Wales. The proposal envisages 900 MW, with IREN targeting a grid connection from 2029. It sits outside the company's secured 5 gigawatt power portfolio and still needs grid and planning approvals. Redbank is therefore an additional development option, not a confirmed part of the build-out — a distinction that does not diminish its potential but stops an early-stage plan from being mentally booked as available capacity. For a capital-intensive project, investors should separate announced scale from secured execution. A large site design is no answer to permitting or financing risk.\n\n## An Unconfirmed Anthropic Link\n\nThe same discipline applies to the reported Anthropic connection. On 12 October, media reports citing people familiar with the relationship described an unannounced multi-year cloud contract with IREN. Neither company confirmed the agreement. Such a report can stir expectations, but it is not enough for a solid valuation. Until confirmation arrives, the potential customer relationship should count neither as a secured order nor as evidence that the build-out is delivering.\n\n## What Would Actually Convince\n\nThe rebound that followed the sell-off, with IREN climbing alongside other technology and AI infrastructure names absent any company-specif","highlights":["IREN dropped 3.8% amid sector-wide AI infrastructure selling; co-CEO says data centre construction was cash-funded with no debt on those sites.\n\n \n\n \n\nIREN's Cash-Funded Build-Out Meets a Market That Wants Receipts Illustration mit AI erstellt.\n\nIREN shares fell 3.8% on the day as renewed selling hit AI data centre and so-called neocloud providers, with worries about oil-driven inflation and higher interest rates setting the tone.
